analysis.one_liner: Writes the FTC's click-to-cancel rule into law, requiring easy subscription cancellation.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 19 House Democrats, has sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee since July 2025 with no hearing, no vote, and no Republican cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: In late 2024 the Federal Trade Commission issued a rule requiring companies that sign people up for recurring subscriptions to make cancelling just as easy as signing up—no phone calls, retention scripts, or in-person visits required. That rule is being challenged in court and could be undone by future administrations. This bill would write the rule into federal law so it could not simply be swept away, and would let the FTC enforce it with the same penalties it uses against unfair and deceptive practices. It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which has taken no further action.
analysis.who_benefits: The millions of households signed up for gyms, streaming services, meal kits, apps, and other subscriptions that are easy to join but hard to leave. The rule requires companies to offer cancellation through the same medium used to sign up, without forcing consumers to navigate obstacles designed to make them give up. If a company makes cancelling difficult, the FTC could seek penalties and refunds for consumers.

how_it_helps.text: Gives the FTC's November 2024 'Negative Option Rule' the force of law, requiring companies that use automatic renewals or free-trial conversions to let consumers cancel as easily as they enrolled [S2].
Lets the FTC enforce the rule as a prohibition on unfair or deceptive practices, meaning violators face FTC Act penalties, including monetary civil penalties and consumer refunds [S2].
Protects the rule from being rescinded by a later administration or narrowed by a court, because a federal statute cannot be undone the way an agency rule can [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Subscription-based businesses—gyms, streaming services, software companies, meal-kit sellers—that profit from customers who keep paying after they wanted out. They face compliance costs to build easy-cancellation systems and FTC enforcement if they fail. A company with no such dependence pays little.
analysis.who_pays_short: Subscription businesses that rely on friction

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on legitimate businesses too: companies must build cancellation systems and keep them working, and the smallest operators may find those costs hardest to absorb [S2].
Writing the rule into law freezes it in its November 2024 form; if experience shows parts of the rule need adjusting, changing them requires a new act of Congress rather than an agency update [S2].

Business groups argue the rule intrudes on private contracts and that some subscription companies offer fair terms; those arguments have kept the underlying rule in legal limbo, which is the problem the bill responds to [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to consumers is real and ongoing: people routinely lose money to subscriptions they meant to cancel, and the rule's core requirement—cancel the way you signed up—is simple and specific. The costs are mainly compliance burdens on businesses, which is the intended trade. The weaker part of the design is the freeze: codifying one dated rule removes the agency's ability to adapt it, though Congress could amend later.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in July 2025 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it has received no hearing, no markup, and no vote, and it remains sitting there while Congress is still in session.

narrative.text: Rep. Brad Sherman introduced the Click to Cancel Act of 2025 on July 29, 2025, joined by Reps. Magaziner and Deluzio [S1][S2].
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, which is the only committee action on record [S4].
19 House Democrats have cosponsored the bill; no Republican has [S3].
No further action—hearing, markup, or floor vote—appears in the action history as of now [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Subscription businesses that profit from hard-to-cancel signups keep their current advantage: the FTC rule is still facing legal and administrative challenge rather than the protection of a federal statute. Consumers who want an easy way out of subscriptions are no better off than before the bill was introduced.

sides.party_line_note: All 19 cosponsors are Democrats; no House Republican has signed on, and the Republican-held committee has taken no action on the bill.

industries.industry: Subscription businesses (gyms, streaming, apps, meal kits)
industries.note: These businesses currently profit from customers who stay enrolled because cancelling is inconvenient. The rule requires cancellation through the same channel used to sign up, eliminating that friction, and FTC penalties back it up.

They face the same compliance requirement as large companies, and building easy-cancellation systems is a proportionally bigger burden for small businesses, though consumers who sign up with them get the same protection.

analysis.trajectory: With no hearing scheduled, no committee action beyond referral, and no Republican cosponsors in a House where Republicans hold a majority, the bill is unlikely to advance this Congress. Its realistic path, if any, would be as an amendment to a broader consumer bill or a restart in a future Congress; the underlying FTC rule it would codify is meanwhile the subject of litigation and administrative review, so the gap this bill would fill persists.
